newsitem.title: USA: Airlines propose security plan to U.S. panel.
newsitem.headline: Airlines propose security plan to U.S. panel.

text.p: Major U.S. airlines on Thursday proposed a plan to a White House panel on aviation security that would deploy explosive detection devices at airports and screen passengers to try to identify terrorists.

"Terrorism has come to our shores and we need to aggressively combat the threat to our nation," said Carol Hallett, president of the Air Transport Association, who presented the ATA's plan to the first hearing of the White House Commission on Aviation Safety and Security.

The panel, chaired by Vice President Al Gore, was set up after the explosion of TWA Flight 800 off New York on July 17, killing all 230 people on board. Investigators have not yet determined the cause but traces of explosive chemicals were found in the wreckage of the B-747, leading them to suspect a bombing or other criminal act.

The ATA plan calls on the commission to announce the immediate deployment for testing of new technology that can trace explosives not now spotted by machines in use at airports. It would also include improved profiles of passengers to try to identify potential terrorists. Airlines reservation systems could be used in the passenger profiles.
Other methods recommended by the ATA included wider use of the FBI in combatting aviation terrorism and increased use of bomb-sniffing dogs for random baggage checks at airports.

Hallett told the panel: "Identifying the threat and using the full power of the government to stop terrorism must be a key element to any security plan. These are measured and aggressive proposals which deserve indeed, demand, your serious consideration."
